stem: A 74-year-old woman is reviewed for long-standing type 2 diabetes and hypertension, both poorly controlled. She has a 5-year history of kidney disease with growing protein loss in the urine and a creatinine clearance now down to 30 mL/min. Her pressure today is 165/95 mm Hg, and she has leg edema. Heart and lung examinations are normal.
oneliner: 74F + T2DM + HTN + 5 y kidney disease + proteinuria + CrCl 30 + leg edema → expected labs vs healthy?
ask: Compared with a healthy person, which set of findings is most likely?

whyNot.A: Failing kidneys make **less** erythropoietin and calcitriol, so neither hematocrit nor calcitriol goes up
whyNot.B: PTH and calcitriol fit, but **CrCl of 30** with years of disease means the kidney's erythropoietin output is also down, so hematocrit falls
whyNot.D: PTH is **raised** by low calcitriol and phosphate retention, not lowered
whyNot.E: With **CrCl 30**, the kidney's hormone jobs are impaired, so nothing stays normal

why: Damaged renal tissue makes **less erythropoietin**, so hematocrit falls, and has **less 1-alpha-hydroxylase**, so calcitriol falls. Low calcitriol and phosphate retention lower serum calcium, which drives **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.
chain: Nephron loss reduces EPO output
Hematocrit falls (normocytic anemia)
1-alpha-hydroxylase activity falls, so calcitriol falls
Phosphate retained, calcium falls
PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism)

idea.rule: Kidney failure means low EPO, low calcitriol and high PTH.
also: End-stage kidney disease on hemodialysis
Anephric patient after bilateral nephrectomy
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis with falling GFR
Lupus nephritis progressing to chronic kidney disease

stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension starts a new loop diuretic and has labs and a volume assessment after 3 days.
oneliner: 61M + HTN + new loop diuretic × 3 days → plasma volume, bicarbonate, pH?
ask: Which set of changes is most likely?

options.A: Plasma volume ↑, serum bicarbonate ↓, arterial pH ↓
options.B: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↓, arterial pH ↓
options.C: Plasma volume ↔, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑
options.D: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑
options.E: Plasma volume ↑, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑

whyNot.A: A diuretic makes him **lose** fluid, so plasma volume does not rise
whyNot.B: Volume is lost, but a loop diuretic does not cause an **acidosis**
whyNot.C: **Three days** of a loop diuretic leaves a net salt and water deficit, so plasma volume does not stay normal
whyNot.E: Alkalosis is right, but the **diuresis** shrinks, not expands, plasma volume

answer: Plasma volume ↓, serum bicarbonate ↑, arterial pH ↑ (contraction alkalosis)
why: Blocking the **Na-K-2Cl cotransporter** causes salt and water loss, so plasma volume falls. The volume loss activates **RAAS**, and aldosterone drives H+ secretion and bicarbonate reabsorption; a smaller extracellular volume also concentrates bicarbonate. The result is **contraction alkalosis**.
chain: Loop blocked in thick ascending limb
Salt and water lost: plasma volume falls
Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system activates
More distal H+ secretion, more HCO3 reabsorbed
Bicarbonate rises, pH rises

idea.rule: Salt and chloride loss that shrinks the ECF, with aldosterone switched on, gives contraction alkalosis.
also: Thiazide diuretics
Vomiting or nasogastric suction
Bartter syndrome (inherited NKCC2 defect)
Gitelman syndrome (inherited NCC defect)
Cystic fibrosis with heavy sweat chloride loss

stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought in for poor growth and constant wet diapers. Her weight and length both sit at the 3rd percentile; she is dehydrated and floppy, and has bowed legs. A slit-lamp examination shows crystals in both corneas. Serum shows low phosphate and low potassium, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urine pH is 5, with glucose, phosphate and amino acids all present in the urine.
oneliner: 18mo F + poor growth + polyuria + bowed legs + corneal crystals + low K, low phosphate + normal-gap acidosis + urine pH 5 + glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria → what causes the acidosis?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her acidosis?

options.A: Failure of H+ secretion by distal intercalated cells
options.B: Reduced bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule
options.C: Aldosterone resistance in the collecting duct
options.D: Excess lactic acid production by tissues
options.E: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition in the distal tubule

whyNot.A: Distal H+ failure cannot acidify urine; hers is **pH 5**, so distal acidification works
whyNot.C: Aldosterone resistance causes **high potassium**; hers is **low**
whyNot.D: Lactate adds unmeasured anions and widens the gap; hers is a **normal gap**
whyNot.E: A distal block would leave **urine pH high**, and she has **glucose and amino acid losses** that point proximal

answer: Reduced proximal bicarbonate reabsorption (renal Fanconi syndrome)
why: Glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate are all reabsorbed in the **proximal tubule**, so losing all of them together means a global proximal defect (**Fanconi syndrome**; **corneal crystals** suggest cystinosis). Bicarbonate wasting causes a **normal-gap acidosis**, and the intact distal nephron can still acidify urine to pH 5.
chain: Cystine builds up in proximal tubule cells
Proximal transport fails
Glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate are lost
Serum bicarbonate falls with a normal anion gap
Distal nephron still acidifies urine (pH 5)

idea.rule: Several solutes lost together in the urine means a proximal tubule defect.
also: Wilson disease
Multiple myeloma light-chain toxicity
Tenofovir or ifosfamide toxicity
Expired tetracycline
Lead poisoning

stem: A 34-year-old woman has had 7 days of watery diarrhea and feels dizzy on standing. Her skin turgor is reduced and her blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Serum Na+ is 136 mEq/L, Cl- 114 mEq/L and HCO3- 15 mEq/L; arterial pH is 7.30.
oneliner: 34F + 7 days watery diarrhea + dizzy, low turgor, BP 98/62 + Na 136, Cl 114, HCO3 15, pH 7.30 → which set of changes?
ask: Which set of changes is most likely?

whyNot.A: A pH of 7.30 with HCO3- 15 calls for **hyperventilation**, so PCO2 falls; a rise would make the acidosis worse
whyNot.B: Low turgor and BP 98/62 show **volume depletion**, which raises aldosterone and ADH and lowers ANP; this is the volume-loaded pattern
whyNot.D: Volume depletion is a strong stimulus for **ADH release**, so ADH rises rather than falls
whyNot.E: The acidosis is **compensated by hyperventilation**, so PCO2 falls; and with the atria less stretched, ANP falls and aldosterone rises

answer: PCO2 and ANP down; aldosterone and ADH up
why: Diarrhea loses **bicarbonate** (gap 136 - 114 - 15 = 7, so a normal anion gap), and the acidosis drives **hyperventilation** so PCO2 falls. Fluid loss means less atrial stretch, so **ANP falls**, while **aldosterone and ADH rise** to save salt and water.
chain: Watery stool loses HCO3- and fluid
HCO3- falls, pH falls: normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis
Chemoreceptors drive faster breathing, so PCO2 falls
Low volume: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH switched on
Less atrial stretch, so ANP is switched off

idea.rule: Bicarbonate loss gives a normal-gap acidosis with a low PCO2, and the volume loss turns aldosterone and ADH up and ANP down.
also: Ileostomy or enteric fistula output
Pancreatic fluid loss
Laxative abuse (with hypokalemia too)
Acetazolamide, which wastes HCO3- in the urine

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had weakness for 2 months. She has taken hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension for 8 years. Lying down, her blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg and pulse 76/min; on standing, 96/64 mm Hg and 102/min. Serum K+ is 3.3 mEq/L.
oneliner: 52F + 8 yrs hydrochlorothiazide + weakness + BP 120/78 → 96/64 and pulse 76 → 102 on standing + K 3.3 → which renal changes?
ask: Which set of renal changes best explains her low potassium?

options.A: Distal Na+ delivery ↑, aldosterone ↑, K+ secretion ↑
options.B: Distal Na+ delivery ↓, aldosterone ↓, K+ secretion ↓
options.C: Distal Na+ delivery ↑, aldosterone ↓, K+ secretion ↑
options.D: Distal Na+ delivery ↓, aldosterone ↑, K+ secretion ↓
options.E: Distal Na+ delivery ↑, aldosterone ↑, K+ secretion ↓

whyNot.B: This pattern would **retain** potassium, but her K+ is low; the thiazide also sends more Na+ downstream, not less
whyNot.C: The **orthostatic fall** in BP with a rising pulse shows volume depletion, which raises aldosterone
whyNot.D: A thiazide blocks Na+-Cl- cotransport in the **early distal tubule**, so more Na+ and fluid reach the collecting duct; low delivery would not waste K+
whyNot.E: Both **more distal flow and aldosterone** push K+ into the urine, so secretion rises; reduced secretion would not leave K+ at 3.3

answer: More distal Na+ delivery and higher aldosterone, so more K+ secreted
why: A thiazide blocks the **Na+-Cl- cotransporter**, so more Na+ and water reach the collecting duct; the **volume loss** (orthostatic drop) raises renin and **aldosterone**. Both increase Na+ uptake through ENaC and **K+ (and H+) secretion** into the lumen.
chain: Thiazide blocks NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
More Na+ and fluid reach the collecting duct; plasma volume falls
Renin and aldosterone rise
ENaC uptake of Na+ makes the lumen negative; K+ is secreted
Urinary K+ loss lowers serum K+

idea.rule: More Na+ and flow reaching the collecting duct plus high aldosterone means K+ (and H+) are wasted.
also: Loop diuretics
Primary hyperaldosteronism
Osmotic diuresis, for example uncontrolled diabetes
Vomiting (volume loss raises aldosterone; bicarbonaturia delivers Na+ distally)
Bartter and Gitelman syndromes

stem: A healthy volunteer sits in a 40°C chamber for 8 hours and drinks no fluid. Plasma osmolality rises to 306 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality reaches 1,000 mOsm/kg. Transport in one nephron segment has been stepped up to help concentrate the urine.
oneliner: Healthy volunteer + 8 h in heat, no fluids + plasma osmolality 306 + urine osmolality 1,000 → which renal transport is stepped up?
ask: Which renal transport process is most likely increased?

options.A: Aquaporin insertion in proximal convoluted tubule cells under ADH
options.B: Water uptake across the thick ascending limb epithelium
options.C: HCO3- recovery by carbonic anhydrase in proximal tubule cells
options.D: Urea transport out of the inner medullary collecting duct
options.E: Glucose uptake by SGLT2 in the early proximal tubule

whyNot.A: ADH acts on V2 receptors of the **collecting duct**; proximal water uptake is by constitutive aquaporin-1 and is not regulated by ADH
whyNot.B: The thick ascending limb is **impermeable to water**; it dilutes the fluid and builds the medullary gradient
whyNot.C: This is **acid-base handling**; a rise in plasma osmolality with concentrated urine does not switch it on
whyNot.E: Glucose uptake follows the **filtered glucose load** and transporter capacity, not hydration state

answer: Urea reabsorption from the inner medullary collecting duct (ADH effect)
why: A rise in plasma osmolality releases **ADH**, which acts on collecting-duct V2 receptors to insert **aquaporin-2** and to upregulate the **UT-A1 urea transporter** in the inner medullary collecting duct. Urea entering the medulla helps hold the gradient that draws water out.
chain: Fluid loss raises plasma osmolality
Osmoreceptors release ADH
V2 receptor: cAMP, aquaporin-2 inserted in collecting-duct cells
Urea transporter (UT-A1) activity rises in the medullary collecting duct
Urea recycling keeps the medulla hypertonic: small volume of concentrated urine

idea.rule: ADH works on the late distal tubule and collecting duct: water through aquaporin-2 and, in the inner medulla, urea through UT-A1.
also: Central diabetes insipidus: no ADH, dilute urine despite high plasma osmolality
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: V2 or aquaporin-2 pathway fails
Urea recycling adds to the medullary gradient that concentrates urine
A low-protein diet lowers medullary urea and weakens maximal concentration

note: Options reworded so no run matches the source option list (RENAL-0133).

stem: A 3-year-old boy has had excessive thirst and large volumes of pale urine since infancy, and his weight is below the 5th percentile. Genetic testing shows a loss-of-function mutation in the vasopressin V2 receptor gene. Water is withheld for 12 hours, then plasma osmolality, serum ADH and urine osmolality are measured.
oneliner: 3M + polyuria, thirst, poor growth + V2 receptor loss-of-function + after 12 h water restriction → which set of values?
ask: Which set of findings is most likely at the end of the test?

options.A: Plasma osmolality ↑, serum ADH ↓, urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg
options.B: Plasma osmolality ↑, serum ADH ↑, urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg
options.C: Plasma osmolality ↑, serum ADH ↑, urine osmolality 600 mOsm/kg
options.D: Plasma osmolality ↓, serum ADH ↓, urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg
options.E: Plasma osmolality ↓, serum ADH ↑, urine osmolality 600 mOsm/kg

whyNot.A: Low ADH would be **central** diabetes insipidus; here the receptor is faulty and the high plasma osmolality drives ADH **up**
whyNot.C: His V2 receptors do not work, so the collecting duct cannot take up water and urine stays **dilute**
whyNot.D: He keeps losing water in urine while drinking nothing, so plasma osmolality **rises**, not falls, and ADH is released
whyNot.E: Low plasma osmolality with concentrated urine is **SIADH**; he is losing free water, so his plasma osmolality is high

answer: Plasma osmolality and ADH up; urine stays dilute
why: With no working **V2 receptor** the collecting duct cannot insert aquaporin-2, so water is lost whatever the **ADH** level. Deprivation then raises plasma osmolality and **ADH**, yet urine osmolality stays near **200** and does not respond to desmopressin.
chain: V2 receptor does not respond
No aquaporin-2 insertion, collecting duct stays water-impermeable
Free water keeps leaving in dilute urine despite deprivation
Plasma osmolality rises
ADH is released in large amounts but cannot act

idea.rule: In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus ADH is high, plasma osmolality is high and urine stays dilute; central DI differs by having low ADH.
also: Central DI: ADH low, urine concentrates after desmopressin
Lithium: reduces aquaporin-2 and ADH signalling
Hypercalcemia and hypokalemia impair concentrating ability
Demeclocycline, used for SIADH, causes NDI as a side effect

stem: A 27-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 3 years and now has marked thirst and passes 6.5 L of urine a day. Serum osmolality is 308 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg. Desmopressin does not change his urine output or osmolality. Tubular fluid is sampled at three sites and compared with plasma.
oneliner: 27M + 3 yrs lithium + thirst + 6.5 L urine/day + serum osm 308, urine osm 85 + no response to desmopressin → tubular fluid osmolality vs plasma?
ask: Which set describes tubular fluid osmolality relative to plasma at the proximal tubule, the macula densa and the medullary collecting duct?

options.A: Proximal isotonic, macula densa isotonic, collecting duct isotonic
options.B: Proximal isotonic, macula densa hypotonic, collecting duct hypertonic
options.C: Proximal hypertonic, macula densa hypotonic, collecting duct hypotonic
options.D: Proximal isotonic, macula densa hypertonic, collecting duct hypotonic
options.E: Proximal isotonic, macula densa hypotonic, collecting duct hypotonic

whyNot.A: The thick ascending limb removes salt without water, so fluid at the **macula densa is hypotonic** whatever ADH is doing
whyNot.B: Collecting-duct fluid only becomes hypertonic when **ADH works**; his urine osmolality is 85 and desmopressin changes nothing
whyNot.C: The proximal tubule takes up solute and water **in step**, so its fluid stays isotonic
whyNot.D: Fluid leaving the thick ascending limb has lost solute without water, so it is **hypotonic**, not hypertonic, at the macula densa

answer: Proximal isotonic; macula densa and collecting duct hypotonic
why: Lithium blocks the ADH pathway in the collecting duct (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), so **water stays in the lumen** and urine osmolality stays at 85. The **proximal tubule** is always isotonic and the **thick ascending limb** always makes the fluid hypotonic; only the collecting duct changes with ADH.
chain: Lithium enters collecting-duct cells and blocks ADH signalling
No aquaporin-2 insertion, collecting duct stays water-tight
Proximal tubule fluid remains isotonic (solute and water move together)
Thick ascending limb dilutes the fluid: hypotonic at the macula densa
Without water leaving, the collecting duct fluid stays hypotonic

idea.rule: Only the collecting duct's tonicity depends on ADH: isotonic at the proximal tubule, hypotonic leaving the thick ascending limb, then hypotonic (no ADH effect) or hypertonic (ADH).
also: Normal concentrating state: collecting-duct fluid becomes hypertonic to plasma
Central DI gives the same tubular pattern as NDI until desmopressin is given
Loop diuretics impair dilution and concentration, bringing fluid at the macula densa closer to isotonic
Primary polydipsia: dilute urine, but ADH is low and concentrating works after restriction

stem: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has 1.2 g/day of urinary protein and a blood pressure of 148/92 mm Hg. Lisinopril is started. Two weeks later his blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg and serum creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.3 mg/dL.
oneliner: 61M + T2DM + proteinuria + BP 148/92 → lisinopril, 2 weeks later BP 130/80 and creatinine 1.1 → 1.3 → which glomerular and hormonal changes?
ask: Which set of changes best describes the drug's effect on his kidneys and hormones?

options.A: GFR ↑, renal plasma flow ↓, filtration fraction ↑, aldosterone ↑
options.B: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↓, filtration fraction ↑, aldosterone ↓
options.C: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↑, filtration fraction ↓, aldosterone ↓
options.D: GFR ↓, renal plasma flow ↑, filtration fraction ↓, aldosterone ↑
options.E: GFR ↔, renal plasma flow ↔, filtration fraction ↔, aldosterone ↓

whyNot.A: This is what **angiotensin II** does (efferent constriction, aldosterone release); the drug removes it, and his rising creatinine points to a lower GFR
whyNot.B: A fall in plasma flow needs **arteriolar constriction**; an ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, so plasma flow rises and filtration fraction falls
whyNot.D: The glomerular half fits, but angiotensin II drives aldosterone release, so blocking its formation makes aldosterone **fall**
whyNot.E: His creatinine **rose**, so GFR changed; efferent dilation drops glomerular pressure and raises plasma flow

answer: GFR down, renal plasma flow up, filtration fraction down, aldosterone down
why: Angiotensin II normally **constricts the efferent arteriole**. Blocking its formation dilates the efferent arteriole, so **plasma flow rises**, glomerular capillary pressure falls and **GFR dips** (the creatinine rise), making the **filtration fraction fall**. **Aldosterone** also falls.
chain: ACE inhibitor lowers angiotensin II
Efferent arteriole dilates
Glomerular capillary pressure falls: GFR falls, creatinine rises
Resistance downstream falls: renal plasma flow rises
GFR falls more than plasma flow rises, so filtration fraction (GFR/RPF) falls; aldosterone falls

idea.rule: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole (raising GFR and filtration fraction); remove it and GFR and filtration fraction fall.
also: ARBs give the same renal effect
Bilateral renal artery stenosis plus an ACE inhibitor can precipitate acute kidney injury
NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole: GFR and plasma flow fall, filtration fraction stays about the same
Efferent constriction by angiotensin II preserves GFR in a low-flow state

stem: In a volunteer with stable GFR and renal plasma flow, p-aminohippurate (PAH) is infused in stepwise increments. PAH secretion rises in proportion to plasma PAH at low levels and then levels off. Point X lies on the rising part of the curve; point Y lies on the plateau, at four times the plasma PAH of X.
oneliner: Volunteer + stable GFR and renal plasma flow + stepwise PAH infusion, secretion rises then plateaus + X on the rising part, Y on the plateau at 4x plasma PAH → which variable is lower at Y?
ask: Which variable is lower at point Y than at point X?

whyNot.B: Filtered load is plasma concentration times GFR; with GFR stable and concentration **four times higher**, it is greater at Y
whyNot.C: Excretion is filtered plus secreted; filtration keeps rising and secretion is at its **maximum**, so excretion is higher at Y
whyNot.D: The stem states that GFR is **stable** across the infusion
whyNot.E: The stem states that renal plasma flow is **stable**

answer: PAH clearance falls above the transport maximum

shifts.var: PAH secretion rate (at its maximum at Y)

why: Clearance is **excretion divided by plasma concentration**. Beyond the **transport maximum**, excretion still rises (more is filtered) but more slowly than plasma PAH, so the ratio falls. Below saturation, PAH clearance estimates renal plasma flow.
chain: Plasma PAH rises past the secretory transport maximum
Secretion plateaus
Excretion rises only through extra filtration
Plasma concentration rises faster than excretion
Clearance (excretion/plasma) falls

idea.rule: Once a transporter saturates, clearance moves toward GFR: a secreted substance's clearance falls and a reabsorbed one's rises.
also: Glucose: reabsorption saturates (about 375 mg/min), so glucose appears in urine and its clearance rises from zero
PAH at low plasma levels is almost completely cleared and estimates renal plasma flow
Inulin clearance stays constant at any plasma concentration because it is only filtered
Probenecid blocks PAH secretion, lowering its clearance toward GFR

stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has a serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL. His physician orders a 24-hour urine collection to calculate creatinine clearance, and notes that it estimates GFR less exactly than inulin clearance does.
oneliner: 52M + long-standing T2DM + creatinine 2.1 + 24 h creatinine clearance planned, less exact than inulin → which property of creatinine limits it?
ask: Which property of creatinine limits its accuracy as a GFR measure?

options.A: It is reabsorbed by the proximal tubule
options.B: It is not freely filtered at the glomerulus
options.C: It is bound to plasma albumin
options.D: It is broken down by tubular cells
options.E: It is secreted by the proximal tubule

whyNot.A: Reabsorption would make clearance **underestimate** GFR; creatinine clearance in practice runs slightly high
whyNot.B: Creatinine is small and **freely filtered**; that is why it can be used at all
whyNot.C: Creatinine is **not significantly protein bound**, so the filtered amount is not reduced
whyNot.D: Creatinine is excreted **unchanged**; tubular metabolism is not the issue

answer: Proximal tubular secretion adds creatinine to the urine, so clearance overestimates GFR

shifts.var: Creatinine clearance compared with true GFR
Inulin clearance compared with true GFR

why: Inulin is **freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted**, so its clearance equals GFR. Creatinine is freely filtered but a little is also **secreted by the proximal tubule**, so its clearance slightly **overestimates GFR**.
chain: Creatinine is freely filtered
A small extra amount is secreted into the proximal tubule
Urinary creatinine exceeds the filtered amount
Clearance (U x V / P) comes out higher than true GFR
Inulin, with no secretion, gives the exact GFR

idea.rule: A GFR marker must be freely filtered with no net secretion or reabsorption; creatinine fails slightly because it is secreted.
also: Cimetidine and trimethoprim block creatinine secretion, raising serum creatinine without a true fall in GFR
In advanced CKD secretion is a larger share, so the overestimate grows
PAH is filtered and secreted almost completely, so it estimates renal plasma flow
Inulin clearance is the reference standard for GFR

stem: In a healthy volunteer on an ordinary diet and fluid intake, the amount of each filtered substance that appears in the urine is compared with the amount that was filtered.
oneliner: Healthy volunteer + normal diet and fluids + amount excreted compared with amount filtered → which substance has the highest fractional excretion?
ask: Which substance has the highest fractional excretion?

whyNot.A: Essentially **all filtered glucose is reabsorbed** below the transport maximum, so its fractional excretion is near zero
whyNot.C: About **99%** of filtered Na+ is reabsorbed, leaving a fractional excretion near 1%
whyNot.D: Roughly **99%** of filtered water is reabsorbed as well, so about 1% is excreted
whyNot.E: Reabsorbed in the proximal tubule under PTH control; only about **5 to 20%** is excreted

answer: Urea, about half of the filtered load
why: Urea is **freely filtered**, then about half is reabsorbed passively with water in the proximal tubule, but it is added back along the loop and reabsorbed again under ADH in the collecting duct. Overall roughly **40 to 60%** of the filtered urea is excreted, far more than the others.
chain: Urea is freely filtered
About half follows water out of the proximal tubule
Medullary recycling adds urea back in the loop
ADH-sensitive collecting-duct uptake
About half of the filtered urea reaches the urine

idea.rule: Fractional excretion shows what is left of the filtered load: glucose near 0, Na+ and water near 1%, phosphate 5-20%, urea about 50%.
also: FENa below 1% in prerenal azotemia
Fractional excretion of urea helps when diuretics make FENa unreliable
BUN rises more than creatinine in volume depletion because more urea is reabsorbed
Glucose fractional excretion rises once its transport maximum is exceeded

stem: A 5-year-old boy has poor growth and a persistent acidosis. Serum Na+ is 140 mEq/L, K+ 3.6 mEq/L, Cl- 112 mEq/L and HCO3- 16 mEq/L; arterial pH is 7.28. His urine pH is 5.0 and urinary ammonium excretion is low. A defect in renal ammonia production is suspected.
oneliner: 5M + poor growth + persistent acidosis + Na 140, Cl 112, HCO3 16, pH 7.28 + urine pH 5.0, low urinary NH4+ → which substrate makes the kidney's ammonia?
ask: Which substrate normally supplies the ammonia made in his kidneys?

whyNot.A: Urea is the **liver's end product** of nitrogen disposal, not a source of renal ammonia
whyNot.B: Made from muscle creatine and **excreted unchanged**; it gives no ammonia to the tubule
whyNot.C: Feeds the **urea cycle** in the liver rather than renal ammoniagenesis
whyNot.E: Used for **heme, purines and creatine**, not the renal ammonia pool

why: Proximal tubule cells take up **glutamine** and deaminate it (glutaminase, then glutamate dehydrogenase) to yield NH4+ and α-ketoglutarate. The NH4+ is secreted into the lumen, where it **traps acid** as ammonium; chronic acidosis raises this production several-fold.
chain: Glutamine enters proximal tubule cells
Glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase release NH4+
NH4+ is secreted into the lumen (NHE3)
Lumen NH4+ carries away H+ and new HCO3- is made
Acidosis upregulates the whole pathway

idea.rule: Renal ammonia comes from glutamine in the proximal tubule and carries acid out of the body as NH4+.
also: Chronic acidosis is met mainly by raising ammoniagenesis
A negative urine anion gap reflects high urinary NH4+, as in diarrhea
A positive urine anion gap in a normal-gap acidosis suggests failed NH4+ excretion, as in renal tubular acidosis
Hyperkalemia suppresses ammoniagenesis (type 4 renal tubular acidosis)
